papers.title: Run One, Get Two: Near-Free Streaming Safety Checks for Local LLMs
papers.abstract: Local LLM assistants decode for one user at a time, so decoding is bound by memory bandwidth and leaves compute idle. Streaming safety checks today trade accuracy against cost. A dedicated guard model is accurate but nearly doubles the latency per token, while a hidden-state probe is cheap but less accurate. We present ToRA, an adapter that runs a second model as an extra row in the generator's decode step, sharing its weights and KV cache. Dual-row kernels read each weight once for both rows. On Qwen3-0.6B, ToRA matches or beats a dedicated streaming guard, with higher F1 on 12 of 17 benchmarks. It detects 11.8 points more unsafe responses than the probe at a similar cost, under 4% added latency per token.

papers.title: PLoQ: A Prompt-Specific Low-Rank Basis for 4-bit Quantization of LLM Activations
papers.abstract: Low-bit activation quantization of large language models remains challenging, as a small number of dominant directions dictate the quantization range. State-of-the-art methods isolate these directions in a high-precision subspace through transformations calibrated offline and folded into the weights, which fixes the subspace for all prompts, leaving each prompt's few unique directions unprotected, and rules it out wherever no weight can absorb the transformation. We present PLoQ, a prompt-adaptive low-rank decomposition that extracts the dominant activation components before quantization, quantizes them separately, and restores them within the layer's GEMM, without modifying the weights. The low-rank component's basis is estimated from each prompt during prefill and reused throughout decoding. At the same bit width as state-of-the-art mixed-precision quantization (4-bit weights, activations and K/V cache with an eighth of the channels at 8 bits, about 4.2 bits per activation on average), PLoQ outperforms it on all six Llama and Qwen models from 1B to 70B parameters, at up to 8k tokens (16k on two of them), recovering up to 46% of the perplexity that the state of the art still loses to 4-bit activations. On Llama-3.1-8B at 8k tokens it adds only 4% to prefill and 8% to decoding.

papers.title: Mosaic: Efficient CPU-GPU Coordinated Block-Sparse Attention
papers.abstract: Long-context LLM serving increasingly relies on CPU-resident context KV cache, driven by KV offloading and disaggregated prefill--decode execution. Although block-sparse attention reduces KV access, existing designs remain inefficient: GPU-centralized execution fetches selected KV blocks from CPU memory at each decoding step, making it PCIe-bound, while CPU--GPU partitioned execution places CPU-side sparse attention on the critical path, leaving substantial GPU time idle. This paper presents Mosaic, a CPU--GPU coordinated block-sparse attention system for efficient long-context decoding with CPU-resident context KV. Mosaic builds on three key insights: output-contribution-aware KV budgeting, head-specific and granularity-aware sparse configuration, and cross-device coordinated scheduling for sparse tasks over CPU-resident KV. Guided by these insights, Mosaic integrates a lightweight head-property predictor, a granularity--budget selector, and a priority-based scheduler to automatically configure and coordinate sparse attention, preserving output quality while improving efficiency on heterogeneous architectures. Across 2 models, 3 benchmarks, and 40 tasks, Mosaic preserves near-FULL quality while achieving a better overall quality--efficiency tradeoff than the evaluated baselines. Compared with the best-quality fixed Quest configuration, Mosaic improves TPOT by up to 3.7$\times$. We further validate Mosaic across four hardware configurations and in a large-model multi-GPU deployment.

papers.title: PennyGS: Full Resolution 3DGS Training in Minutes on Consumer GPUs
papers.abstract: 3D Gaussian Splatting is increasingly fed by high-resolution captures from commodity devices, yet training still happens at reduced resolution with research-grade GPUs. We present PennyGS, a method to achieve full-resolution (4K) training of 3DGS on consumer GPUs by improving the efficiency of every stage of a training step. Improvements include a leaner splat with flat RGB color and a directional cone opacity, fused projection and key emission, forward rasterization optimizations with strided pixel sampling, an approximate tile SSIM loss, a warp-per-splat backward rasterization, and a fused backward projection and sparse Adam step. At the standard 30k-step budget, PennyGS is the fastest of 10 methods on Mip-NeRF 360 and Tanks&Temples 4K on all four GPUs at competitive quality, at least 3.9x faster than the quickest of the others, while peaking below 2 GB of GPU memory. On an RTX 3060, a full-resolution Mip-NeRF 360 scene trains in 6m 25s, faster than any other method trains it on an RTX 4090.

papers.title: Drive Failure and Lifetime Simulation in the Backblaze Drive Statistics Corpus, 2013-2026
papers.abstract: Storage simulators estimate data-loss risk from assumptions about drive lifetimes and dependence between failures. We test these assumptions against Backblaze's daily records from April 2013 to June 2026: 504,624 data drives with usable power-on ages, 99 drive models, 2.0 million drive-years and 31,881 recorded failures, including removals of drives judged likely to fail. We test failure-count forecasts over nine successive years and forecast the drives already in service at each prediction date. Accounting for drive-model differences and attributes improves the score assigned to observed failure counts about 4.3 times as much as replacing a single Weibull with two competing Weibulls under the same drive-model treatment. Fleet failure risk falls early and rises at older ages, but the fixed bathtub benchmark predicts 2.4 times the observed failures. Across 169 well-observed drive-model years selected using earlier records, 95% prediction intervals cover 44% of observed counts without annual variation and 92% with fleet-wide changes and shared good or bad years for each drive model. For drives already in service, a SMART warning raises one-year failure-risk ranking AUC from 0.64 to 0.73. Boosted trees using monthly SMART records give the best individual probability forecasts, yet predict 19% too many failures at one year and 22% too many at 90 days. Long-term survival depends on how aging is separated from calendar time: fitted fifteen-year survival probabilities differ by up to 18 percentage points, and assumptions about future calendar trends by up to 27 points. We provide samplers for storage simulations that represent drive-model differences, shared risks, and changes in drive condition.
